title: Wi-Fi 5 vs Wi-Fi 6 vs Wi-Fi 7
summary: Wi-Fi 6 introduced OFDMA and 1024-QAM for crowded environments, while Wi-Fi 7 introduces 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, and Multi-Link Operation (MLO).

body.definition: A Wi-Fi 7 feature allowing a client device to simultaneously transmit and receive data across multiple frequency bands (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, 6 GHz) over a single aggregated connection.

body.text: Wi-Fi standards evolve through IEEE 802.11 working group amendments. While Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) focused primarily on single-device raw speed over 5 GHz, Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) revolutionized multi-device efficiency using OFDMA. Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) pushes theoretical throughput past 40 Gbps with ultra-low latency.
Generational Comparison
OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) divides a Wi-Fi channel into dozens of sub-carriers, letting a router talk to multiple devices simultaneously.

title: Wi-Fi Frequency Bands: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz & 6 GHz
summary: 2.4 GHz penetrates walls effectively at lower speeds, 5 GHz offers high bandwidth over moderate distances, and 6 GHz provides wide, uncongested channels.

body.definition: The electromagnetic wave frequency range utilized by wireless communications, where higher frequencies carry more data per second but attenuate faster through solid materials.

body.text: The 2.4 GHz band is crowded with Bluetooth, microwaves, and legacy IoT devices, and only has three non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (1, 6, 11). The 5 GHz band expands channel capacity significantly, while the newer 6 GHz band (Wi-Fi 6E/7) opens up 1,200 MHz of clean spectrum with zero interference from older legacy routers.
Band Tradeoffs
Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) requires 5 GHz routers to switch channels if they detect nearby airport or military weather radar signals.

title: Mesh Wi-Fi Networks & Seamless Roaming
summary: A mesh network uses multiple interconnected wireless nodes sharing a single SSID to blanket large homes with seamless 802.11k/v/r roaming.

body.definition: A decentralized communications network composed of radio nodes that organize dynamically, passing traffic across intermediate hops back to the primary gateway router.

body.text: Traditional Wi-Fi extenders repeat signals on separate SSIDs, cutting bandwidth in half and causing devices to cling stubbornly to distant weak signals. Mesh systems use a single unified network name (SSID), coordinating handoffs smoothly using standardized roaming protocols.
Roaming Standards

items: 802.11k (Radio Resource Measurement): Creates an optimized neighbor report so phones know which adjacent node has the best signal without full-band scanning.
802.11v (BSS Transition Management): The router actively advises clients to migrate to a less congested access point.
802.11r (Fast BSS Transition): Caches encryption handshake keys across nodes so authentication takes under 50ms without audio dropouts.

body.text: Tri-band mesh systems dedicate a second 5 GHz or 6 GHz radio exclusively for wireless backhaul communication between satellite nodes.

title: Wi-Fi Calling (VoWiFi)
summary: Wi-Fi Calling routes voice calls and SMS text messages over an encrypted IPSec Internet tunnel directly to your mobile carrier's IMS core.

body.definition: A 3GPP telecommunications standard that enables cellular voice calls and SMS to traverse standard IP broadband networks through secure ePDG gateways into the carrier IMS network.

body.text: When cellular reception is obstructed by thick concrete walls or basement shielding, VoWiFi seamlessly bridges your phone to the cellular provider over standard home Wi-Fi. It uses the same dialer, caller ID, and high-definition AMR-WB codecs as VoLTE.
VoWiFi Architecture

items: IKEv2 & IPSec Tunnel: Establishes an end-to-end encrypted VPN tunnel between the handset and the carrier's Evolved Packet Data Gateway (ePDG).
SIM Authentication: Uses the physical or eSIM cryptographic credentials (EAP-AKA) to verify carrier subscriber identity.
Seamless Handover: Calls hand over bidirectionally between VoWiFi and VoLTE without disconnecting as signal strength fluctuates.

body.text: VoWiFi does not require any third-party app (like WhatsApp or Skype) and routes directly to regular telephone numbers worldwide.

title: Physical SIM vs eSIM (eUICC)
summary: An eSIM is a miniature chip permanently soldered to the motherboard that can be reprogrammed over-the-air with multiple carrier network profiles.

body.definition: A hardware secure element conforming to GSMA remote SIM provisioning specifications that allows digital cellular profiles to be downloaded securely via SM-DP+ servers.

body.text: Traditional SIM cards require physical plastic trays and nano-SIM cards. An eSIM replaces this mechanical tray with a tiny surface-mount chip (SON-8 package), freeing up valuable internal smartphone space for larger batteries and improved IP68 water resistance.
Key Differences

rows.label: Provisioning
values: Instant QR code or carrier app push

rows.label: Theft Security
values: Thief can eject SIM to disable tracking
Cannot be physically removed from stolen device

body.text: Dual eSIM functionality allows modern phones to keep two digital carrier profiles active simultaneously on separate IMEI transceivers.

title: Mobile Hotspot & Tethering
summary: Mobile hotspot routing turns your smartphone into a portable wireless router using NAT and packet forwarding across cellular and Wi-Fi interfaces.

body.definition: A network routing process where a mobile operating system creates a private local subnet (DHCP server) and rewrites packet headers to bridge connected clients to the cellular WAN.

body.text: When you turn on a mobile hotspot, the OS launches a local Wi-Fi Access Point (AP) mode daemon, starts a dnsmasq DHCP service, and activates Linux iptables kernel packet forwarding between the cellular interface (rmnet_data0) and wireless interface (wlan0).
Tethering Modes Compared

items: Wi-Fi Hotspot: Supports multiple simultaneous clients; highest battery consumption.
USB Tethering: Direct USB network adapter (RNDIS/NCM); lowest latency, zero wireless interference, charges phone simultaneously.
Bluetooth Tethering: Ultra-low power consumption (PAN profile); capped at roughly 1-2 Mbps bandwidth.

body.text: Carriers can inspect the IP packet Time-To-Live (TTL) field to distinguish native smartphone traffic from tethered laptop hotspot traffic.

title: Carrier Aggregation (LTE-A & 5G NR)
summary: Carrier Aggregation combines multiple distinct cellular frequency bands into a single high-bandwidth data channel to boost peak download speeds.

body.definition: A core feature of LTE-Advanced and 5G NR that bundles two or more component carriers across identical or distinct frequency bands into a unified virtual transmission pipe.

body.text: In standard 4G, a phone communicates over a single 10 MHz or 20 MHz spectrum slice. With Carrier Aggregation (represented by the '4G+' or '5G+' icon), a modem can aggregate three to five different frequency bands simultaneously (e.g. Band 3 1800MHz + Band 7 2600MHz + Band 20 800MHz), multiplying peak throughput.
Aggregation Types

items: Intra-band Contiguous: Combining adjacent frequency channels within the exact same frequency band.
Intra-band Non-contiguous: Combining separate channels within the same spectrum band.
Inter-band Non-contiguous: Aggregating completely distinct spectrum bands (e.g., low-band 700 MHz coverage with mid-band 3.5 GHz capacity).

body.text: Carrier aggregation requires sophisticated RF front-end modules (switches, duplexers, and power amplifiers) to prevent internal intermodulation harmonic distortion.
